description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Bing Yi, Shiyu Liu, Wei He, Xiaorui Chen, Xu Cao, Wei Kang, Xianjiang Zeng, Xian-ge Wang, Bing Zhou, Liang Zhu, Fei Liu
abstract: Surface water-groundwater interactions (SGI) zones act as critical biogeochemical hotspots regulating the transport and transformation of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in alpine watersheds, where seasonal precipitation and snowmelt influence carbon cycles by modulating SGI patterns. To elucidate these complex hydro-biogeochemical linkages within a representative alpine context, optical indices, molecular characteristics, and stable water isotopes were combined to investigate DOM sources, composition, and transformation in surface water and groundwater in the Datonghe watershed, a typical high-altitude catchment in the northeastern Tibetan Plateau characterized by intense and climate-sensitive SGI. The main findings showed that DOM in groundwater predominantly recharged by precipitation (GRP) exhibited lower aromaticity and double bond equivalents (DBEwa = 7.4), higher S275-295 values (15.46 ± 9.77 μm−1), and enrichment in aliphatic compounds and peptides. In contrast, surface water and non-GRP groundwater were dominated by aromatic hydrocarbons and carboxyl-rich alicyclic molecules (CRAM) with higher molecular weights. Notably, GRP contained five times more high-oxygen sulfur compounds (O/S > 12) than other water types, suggesting oxidative inputs from atmospheric aerosols. Overall, precipitation intensity drove DOM dynamics by activating distinct SGI pathways. SGI functioned as bidirectional yet asymmetrical biogeochemical regulator. Although vertical recharge during intense rainfall delivered photochemically oxidized, aliphatic-rich atmospheric signatures into the aquifer, lateral transport drove intensive redox-mediated nitrogen and sulfur transformations. Consequently, whereas groundwater underwent robust molecular reworking, the riverine DOM pool remained shaped by the mixing of recalcitrant, subsurface-processed groundwater end-members. Therefore, hydrological connectivity and recharge pathways exerted first-order controls on DOM oxidation, redox turnover, and carbon mobility across the surface water–groundwater continuum.

title: Advancing the calibration of macroscale hydrological models by integrating sensitivity analysis, adaptive pseudo-modeling optimization and multi-site calibration
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Chandni Thakur, Venkatesh Budamala, K.S. Kasiviswanathan, Claudia Teutschbein, Bankaru-Swamy Soundharajan
abstract: Accurate estimation of parameters in macroscale, complex hydrological models (HMs) using effective calibration procedures can improve the characterization of real-world phenomena of hydrological fluxes. This study presents a novel, model-agnostic calibration framework that integrates global sensitivity analysis (SA) with an adaptive pseudo-modelling optimization strategy. The framework is designed to overcome key limitations of conventional calibration methods, such as reliance on exhaustive one-shot sampling, absence of formal parameter screening, and restriction to single site calibration. To demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework, catchment-specific sensitive parameters of the variable infiltration capacity model (VIC) with a 0.15° spatial resolution were calibrated for streamflow simulations over the Godavari River basin in India using both single- and multi-site calibration. An ensemble of pseudo models, including Gaussian process regression, kriging, and artificial neural networks, was employed to enhance robustness and generalization. Although the performance indicators (NSE, KGE ≥ 0.8 and PBIAS ≤ 15) in both scenarios demonstrated similar model performance at the catchment outlet, scenario 2 outperformed single-site calibration in terms of equifinality reduction, less parameter uncertainty and improved computational efficiency. By combining Sobol SA, ensemble pseudo modelling, and multi-site calibration, the framework efficiently explored hydrologically relevant regions of the parameter space, reduced dimensionality by excluding non-influential parameters, and lowered overall computational burden. The proposed framework is a robust method for improving the simulation capability of macroscale HMs under diverse hydroclimatic conditions. Plain language summary Hydrological models, such as the VIC model, are powerful computer-based tools used to study and understand water movement on a local to large scale, particularly at the river basin scale. The calibration process involves adjusting the model’s parameters to ensure that the model outputs align with real-world observations. Improving the calibration of hydrological models, like VIC, enhances their ability to make reliable predictions, which is vital for effective water resource management and decision-making. This paper presents a novel hybrid modelling framework combining sensitivity analysis and an adaptive optimization algorithm to calibrate complex hydrological models automatically. The proposed approach can be a robust and time-efficient method for improving large-scale hydrological models, enabling decision-makers to make informed choices and develop effective strategies for addressing water-related challenges.

title: Station-based assessment of reanalysis surface air temperature and warming trends over the Tibetan Plateau (1980–2018)
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Shun Zhang, Zhiguo Li, Ning Xu, Yongqiang Zhang, Xinyu Zhu, Yetang Wang
abstract: The Tibetan Plateau (TP), one of the most climate-sensitive and hydrologically crucial regions on Earth, poses significant challenges for the accurate estimation of surface air temperature. In this study, we evaluate five widely used global reanalysis datasets (ERA-Interim, JRA-55, MERRA-2, ERA5, ERA5-Land) against observations from 132 meteorological stations during 1980–2018. For daily temperature accuracy, the overall ranking is JRA-55 > ERA-Interim > ERA5 > MERRA-2 > ERA5-Land. JRA-55 and ERA5 provide the most reliable overall representation of warming trends over the TP. The observed median annual warming trend is about 0.45 °C/decade, with the strongest warming in winter (0.47 °C/decade). All five reanalysis datasets show negative trend biases, indicating systematic underestimation of observed warming. Errors are largest in winter and are consistently concentrated in the topographically complex and monsoon-influenced southeastern TP, a hydrologically important headwater region. The post-2000 warming dipole, characterized by accelerated warming in the southeast and relative slowdown toward the northeastern TP, is reproduced best by JRA-55 and ERA-Interim and is weakest in MERRA-2. Overall, JRA-55 provides the highest overall accuracy, while JRA-55 and ERA5 provide the most reliable representation of warming trends over the TP.

title: Multivariate design storms using vine copulas and Gaussian process regression
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Diego Urrea Méndez, Dina Vanessa Gómez Rave, Manuel del Jesus
abstract: Multivariate design storms represent events associated with a defined Joint Return Period (JRP) while preserving observed spatial dependence. They enable the synthetic generation of storms that have not yet been observed but are plausibly likely, thereby expanding the scenario space for design and risk assessment. Two practical challenges persist: (i) embedding JRPs within storm-generation procedures beyond three dimensions, which is computationally demanding; and (ii) representing spatial intermittency, which has so far been treated only with a bivariate Multivariate Mixture Model (MMM). We present a method that addresses both challenges concurrently. We compare five copula-based approaches for high-dimensional dependence, employ Gaussian process regression (GPR) to accelerate JRP estimation, and extend the MMM to represent intermittency in multiple dimensions. The framework is applied to the Besaya River basin (northern Spain). Results show that GPR reduces computational cost by an order of magnitude while maintaining approximation errors on the order of 10 − 3 , and that the MMM captures intermittency in multidimensional settings. Flexible vine copula–based approaches best preserve spatial and multidimensional dependence in multivariate storm generation, whereas Gaussian-based and univariate benchmarks systematically underestimate storm totals.

title: Integrating multiple graph features in graph neural networks for water level prediction
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Ruojing Zhang, Sen Ju, Zhengli Yao
abstract: Accurate and rapid water level prediction plays an important role in water resource management and flood prevention. Existing studies usually rely on the geographical location of hydrological stations for modelling, while this single spatial perspective may not adequately reflect the complexity and diversity of water level changes. On this basis, similarity relationship among hydrological time series can provide richer spatial and temporal information. This study proposes a GNN framework called Fused Multi-Graph Temporal Graph Neural Network (FMG-TGNN), which captures spatio-temporal dependencies by constructing multiple graph structures and integrating them to enhance the accuracy of water level prediction. Specifically, three distinct graph structures are constructed based on the hydrological linkage, the Pearson correlation coefficient, and the Dynamic Time Warping (DTW). Chebyshev graph convolution (ChebConv) is then applied to each of these structures to extract features. These extracted features are subsequently fused through a learnable weighted summation and then concatenated with the raw data and fed into the GRU layer. This process enables effective capture and integration of spatiotemporal dependencies. The proposed framework is evaluated using data from 13 hydrological monitoring stations in Changzhou. The experimental results show that the framework performs well in both single-step and multi-step short-term water level forecasting, validating its effectiveness in improving the accuracy of water level prediction.

title: Spatiotemporal evolution, physical drivers, and future prediction of global terrestrial moisture imbalance: a multi-expert AI-agent approach based on SVBI
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Longhao Xu, Kebiao Mao, Zhonghua Guo, Jiancheng Shi, Sayed M. Bateni, Zijin Yuan
abstract: Global warming intensifies terrestrial moisture imbalance (vapor supply–demand mismatch), while traditional indices exhibit limitations in capturing flash anomalies induced by water vapor dynamic feedback. This study proposes the Standardized Vapor Balance Index (SVBI) and a collaborative framework based on AI-Agent routing and multi-expert systems to systematically analyze global moisture imbalance evolution, physical drivers, and projections from 1979 to 2024. Results demonstrate a physical decoupling between SVBI and SPEI (R = 0.185), with SVBI exhibiting superior sensitivity to flash signals. Global imbalance displays pronounced seasonality, the summer grid trend reaches 0.277 decade−1 , while the North Frigid Zone winter shows a negative evolution (−0.213 decade−1 ) under polar locking. Extreme events feature “high intensity and long duration,” with a tropical peak severity of 6.36 and a maximum duration of 5.40 months in the North Frigid Zone. Nonlinear attribution identifies TCWV as the dominant variable (21.3% contribution), with summer imbalance governed by dynamic processes (70%) and winter strictly constrained by thermodynamics. Projections across three emission scenarios (SSP1-2.6, 2–4.5, 5–8.5) via the Agent-Expert framework reveal a risk landscape of “northern intensification and southern stability.” Regional peak intensities, particularly in mid-to-high latitudes, consistently exceed the 3.0 high-risk threshold, with North Frigid Zone variability reaching 0.878, signaling systemic non-stationarity in high-latitude moisture cycles. These findings inform global moisture risk monitoring and regional water resource management.

title: A hierarchical hybrid flood modeling framework: deconstructing runoff response into initiation states and generation processes
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Tao Xie, Lu Chen, Bin Yi, Zhiyuan Leng, Siming Li, Yazhong Wu, Deming Zhu
abstract: Catchment runoff response physically entails two hierarchical phases: runoff initiation and runoff generation mechanisms. However, existing hydrological models rarely capture the temporal dynamics and process heterogeneity of both phases simultaneously. This simplification forces models to adapt to varying hydrological behaviors using static structures and parameters, inevitably leading to structural deficiencies and parameter compensation. To address this, we propose a Hierarchical Hybrid Flood Modeling Framework implemented through three progressive components. First, a two-stage flood event partitioning protocol is established to define runoff initiation states using physical thresholds and discriminate dominant runoff generation mechanisms via hypothesis testing. Second, an interpretable machine learning module is developed to dynamically recognize these hydrological categories based on real-time rainfall characteristics and antecedent catchment conditions. Third, a flexible hydrological modeling architecture incorporating multiple runoff generation mechanisms is constructed to adaptively simulate the identified physical processes based on recognition results. Application in the Han River basin demonstrates substantial performance improvements over traditional models, increasing the validation Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency from 0.62 to 0.68, 0.77 to 0.80, 0.62 to 0.64, and 0.73 to 0.80 across the four catchments, respectively. Furthermore, SHAP-based interpretability analysis confirms the physical realism of the framework by elucidating the controlling factors for both runoff initiation thresholds and distinct runoff generation mechanisms. By reconciling the conflict between static model structures and dynamic hydrological processes, this framework achieves simulation results that are more consistent with the actual physical processes of the catchment.

title: Goodness-of-fit can be misleading: probability plots
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Xiaoyang Li, Brent Boehlert, Richard M. Vogel, Lei Ye
abstract: When modeling the relationship between the frequency and magnitude of a natural hazard, there is a need to select and fit a probability distribution function (pdf) that mimics the unknown parent distribution. Goodness-of-fit metrics are often used to assess how well a hypothesized pdf fits observations. The goal of such evaluations is to ensure that the chosen pdf reproduces various important properties associated with the correct pdf. The probability plot correlation coefficient (PPCC) test based on a quantile–quantile (Q–Q) probability plot is a widely used tool for evaluating the goodness-of-fit of a hypothesized pdf to a sample of observations. Among 200 flood series from rivers in the U.S. with very long records, it was generally only those rivers that experienced extraordinary floods, which led to very low PPCC values, raising questions about the value of the PPCC statistic. Monte Carlo experiments reveal that the PPCC goodness-of-fit metric based on a Q–Q probability plot, is highly sensitive to outliers, and as a result can be quite misleading, causing us to reject the correct pdf in situations when it would have been very important to identify it as the distribution most consistent with the observations. Variable transformations for Q–Q plots and PPCC goodness-of-fit metrics based on probability-probability (P–P) plots are shown to give a much more balanced assessment of a hypothesized pdf. Our findings apply to any natural hazard which exhibits heavy tailed behavior.

title: Investigation of sediment incipient velocity in ice-covered flow under slope effects and dual riverbed roughness boundary conditions
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Shaomin Meng, Xiaomin Liu, Tingxi Liu, Anjun Deng, Hai Huang
abstract: The formation of ice covers over rivers in cold regions can substantially change hydraulic boundary conditions and the dynamic structure of river flows, thereby affecting sediment erosion and deposition processes and escalating the risk of ice flooding. Conventional open-channel flow theory has notable limitations in forecasting sediment incipient motion under ice cover, especially with respect to slope effects. Using theoretical analysis, model development and slope-varying flume experiments, this study systematically examines the incipient velocity laws for non-uniform sediment, accounting for slope effects under ice cover and dual riverbed roughness boundary conditions. It establishes a probabilistic model of sediment incipient motion that integrates slope and the relative exposure randomness of particles. In addition, this research proposes a mid-perpendicular average flow velocity formula applicable to both open-channel and ice-covered flow conditions. The root-mean-square errors of the model and the formula were 0.01973 m/s and 0.01279 m/s, respectively, further demonstrating good predictive accuracy. The experiments revealed a distinctive phenomenon – incipient motion at a low Froude number – in ice-covered flow, driven by enhanced bed shear stress and the increased energy efficiency at the riverbed surface, which collectively reduce the macroscopic hydrodynamic force required for incipient motion. The dominant effect of the ratio of dual riverbed roughness coefficients (ni /nc ) was further quantified by defining the ice cover influence factor (ICIF). Notably, ICIF intensified significantly with increasing ni /nc . In addition, fine sediments were more sensitive to variations in ni /nc . The parameter sensitivity analysis demonstrated that particle size exerted the greatest influence on incipient velocity, followed by slope and ice cover roughness. Among these factors, particle size was the absolutely dominant variable. This study delves into the mechanism of sediment incipient motion in ice-covered flows and provides theoretical support for predicting sediment transport and regulating ice floods in frozen rivers.

title: HydroCraft: an efficient online platform for hydrological modeling integrated with a large language model agent
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Mahmut Tudaji, Fuqiang Tian, Xiannan Wu
abstract: Hydrological modeling is essential for water resources management but often requires specialized expertise, creating a significant barrier to its broad application. To address this challenge, we developed HydroCraft, a web-based platform designed to democratize the modeling process. HydroCraft provides a comprehensive and integrated workflow for basin extraction, driving data generation, parameter calibration, and result visualization, enabling rapid modeling for any watershed globally. Key features of the platform include: an adaptive watershed delineation method that optimizes the distribution of computational units based on user-defined sub-basin area thresholds; the integration of three hydrological models (THREW, Xin’anjiang, and Miyun Hydrological Model) suitable for diverse climatic and geological conditions; and the incorporation of a Large Language Model (LLM) agent, which serves as a robust assistant to provide guidance and automated task execution. Users only need a device with a web browser and an internet connection to perform advanced hydrologic simulations. Two case studies (user-driven vs. LLM-agent-assisted) demonstrated the platform’s efficiency and intelligence. The platform advances hydrological modeling toward greater intelligence and accessibility, providing support for applications such as water resource management and flood forecasting.

title: Decoupling of evapotranspiration from atmospheric demand: mechanistic insights into the local evaporation paradox in arid shrublands via physical and physiological resistance thresholds
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Yuquan Qiang, Mingjun Zhang, Yu Zhang, Shengjie Wang, Xianying Xu, Jinchun Zhang, Guiquan Fu, Zhilan Wang, Meilin Sun, Peng Zhao, Shiquan Liu
abstract: Accurate quantification of hydrological fluxes in arid ecosystems is fundamental for modeling regional water cycle dynamics under progressive global aridification. Modeling these fluxes is complicated by the ’evaporation paradox,’ a hydro-meteorological anomaly where actual evapotranspiration (ET) stagnates or declines despite rising atmospheric evaporative demand. Existing land surface models often lack the capacity to resolve the complex, nonlinear interactions between sparse vegetation canopies and soil water deficits. To address these structural limitations, we propose a Physiologically Constrained Shuttleworth-Wallace (PC-SW) two-source model tailored for temperate desert shrublands (Haloxylon ammodendron). The model integrates three physical modifications: (1) A piecewise linear soil resistance function was formulated to account for the disruption of liquid water continuity in shallow soil layers during desiccation, capturing the abrupt ’two-stage switching’ effect triggered by dry surface layer (DSL) formation. (2) A hydraulic-stomatal regulation module, incorporating deep root zone moisture signals and Leaf Area Index (LAI) thresholds, was established to quantitatively characterize plant “physiological dormancy” under extreme drought. (3) A clumping index correction based on geometric optics was applied to rectify radiative transfer errors associated with patchy shrub canopies. Model performance was evaluated using high-frequency eddy covariance and sap flow data collected across two growing seasons (2023–2024) in the Minqin Oasis-Desert Transition Zone, China. Results indicate that the PC-SW model mitigates the systematic overestimation of soil evaporation inherent in the standard S-W model (reducing bias by ∼ 45%) and achieves high simulation accuracy (R2 > 0.90). Hydrological flux partitioning indicated that plant transpiration serves as the primary pathway for ecosystem water loss—contributing over 96% during the peak growing season—and is sustained largely by deep soil water reservoirs (40–300 cm). This analysis explicitly identifies the localized thermodynamic feedbacks driving the evaporation paradox. While the concept of “functional decoupling” induced by high surface resistance is recognized in ecohydrology, this study advances its predictive modeling by mathematically formalizing the specific physical and physiological thresholds that trigger this process. By incorporating a piecewise linear soil resistance model and an explicit dormancy threshold, the PC-SW model better captures the abrupt restriction of actual ET under severe water limitation. Consequently, excess radiant energy is preferentially partitioned into sensible heat, providing a mechanistic, threshold-driven explanation for the local evaporation paradox.

title: Quantifying heterogeneous hydrological interactions in complex river basins: an interpretable spatiotemporal deep learning approach
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Jie Lin, Wei Ding, Huicheng Zhou, Jing Hu, Hao Wang
abstract: Hydrological regimes in complex river basins are governed by heterogeneous hydrological interactions, including driver-to-response interactions induced by multi-source inflows and response-to-response interactions within basin-scale hydrological processes. These interactions are essential for guiding scientific river-basin regulation, while their systematic quantification remains challenging, constrained by computation-intensive modeling and scenario-limited analysis. To this end, this study develops an Interpretable Spatio-Temporal Hydrological Interaction Learning (InSTIL) framework, which combines LSTM-based temporal encoding, graph-based spatial propagating and Shapley Additive Explanations, to explicitly capture and quantify the hydrological interactions. Applied to the Three Gorges Reservoir (TGR) and Dongting Lake (DTL) system, InSTIL delivers robust simulations of lake water levels with an average RMSE of 0.425 m, consistently outperforming LSTM and GCN benchmarks, particularly under extreme conditions. Furthermore, interaction interpretation reveals that: (1) For driver-to-response interactions between rivers and the lake, their spatial patterns from different rivers are governed by inflow locations and runoff volumes, with TGR releases exerting the dominant influence (contributing 32.89%-48.58% across individual sites) and tributary Yuan River ranking second. Meanwhile, these interactions appear unimodal over time, showing the strongest daily impacts at 1–3 days before lake’s responses. Their multi-day cumulative effects inform an effective regulation window of 7–15 days. (2) For response-to-response interactions within the lake, the heterogeneous response timing and magnitude across DTL reveal the weak hydraulic connectivity in the south sub-lake and the presence of a cross-sublake hydraulic pathway. Overall, InSTIL provides a transferable paradigm for robust hydrological simulations and systematic interaction interpretation, offering practical insights for sustainable river-basin management.

title: FlowGATFormer: A streamflow prediction model based on spatiotemporal dual attention
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Feng Liu, Zhigang Han, Jingru Ma, Peiqing Xiao, Pan Zhang, Fengrui Chen, Xiang Yu
abstract: Achieving high accuracy in long-term river streamflow prediction is essential for simulating the terrestrial hydrological cycle and managing water resources. However, traditional hydrological models are often computationally expensive and require complex parameter estimation and calibration. Deep learning models, particularly long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have shown promise in streamflow forecasting, but their predictive accuracy tends to decrease at longer forecast horizons. To address these issues, this study proposes FlowGATFormer, a streamflow forecasting model that integrates a graph attention network (GAT) with the Informer architecture. The model introduces a dual spatiotemporal attention to capture spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics in river systems. FlowGATFormer is applied to predict streamflow at five forecast horizons including 1, 6, 12, 16, and 24 days ahead. Specifically, the GAT models spatial dependencies among hydrological stations located upstream and downstream of a river network, while the Informer captures temporal dependencies within long-term streamflow series derived from the same hydrological station. Based on data from 11 stations in the CAMELS-CH dataset (1999–2020), FlowGATFormer significantly outperforms baseline models by achieving a Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.5616 (NSE > 0.5) for the 12-day-ahead prediction. Compared to the LSTM baseline, the NSE improvement gradually increases with the prediction horizon, rising from 3.09% for the 6-day-ahead prediction to 10.98% for the 24-day-ahead prediction. We believe that the FlowGATFormer has the potential to be a robust data-driven approach for high-accuracy, long-term river streamflow prediction.

title: Using stable isotopes in water vapor to identify the onset date of the East Asian summer monsoon over the Loess Plateau
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Yujiao Zhang, Yudong Shi, Shengjie Wang, Hayoung Bong, Kei Yoshimura, Shijun Lei, Meng Xing, Yinmei Yang, Jianwen Zhao, Mingjun Zhang
abstract: The East Asian summer monsoon (EASM) is a key atmospheric circulation system that regulates the hydroclimatic patterns and ecological processes of the Loess Plateau. Its onset date has important implications for the seasonal distribution of regional precipitation, water resource allocation, and land–atmosphere interactions. In this study, we developed a quantitative framework for identifying monsoon onset based on the daily time series of water vapor δ 18O. Using observed water vapor isotope records from Lanzhou and Xi’an across the Loess Plateau, we determined a robust onset signal characterized by a maximum in δ 18O followed by sustained isotopic depletion. After applying a 10-day Fourier low-pass smoothing, objective criteria with a cumulative decrease of at least 2‰ were established to identify the monsoon onset date. This framework was further applied to long-term daily isotope simulations of IsoGSM4 to reconstruct the interannual variability of EASM onset over the Loess Plateau. The results show that the summer monsoon typically reaches the Loess Plateau in June and exhibits a stable southeast-to-northwest propagation pattern. On average, monsoon onset occurs in Xi’an in early June, whereas Lanzhou lags by approximately 15–20 days. The inter-annual variability of monsoon onset date is consistent with recent evidence for a northward shift of the East Asian rain belt. This isotope-based framework provides a robust quantitative indicator for identifying EASM onset across the Loess Plateau, and helps in understanding the long-term hydrological changes in the monsoon marginal regions.

title: Scale-specific controls of annual suspended sediment yield in Yellow River Basin
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Zhongming Chen, Sixiao Zhang, Wenhai Shi, Juan Zhao
abstract: Sediment transport is inherently multi-scale and nonlinear, driven by interactions among meteorological, hydrological and ecological processes. However, the scale-dependent relationships between sediment yield and its potential drivers remain poorly understood since multiple underlying mechanisms overlap at the observational scale. To address this gap, this study applies multivariate empirical mode decomposition (MEMD) to identify the scale-specific controls on sediment production. Annual sediment yield and five influencing factors—runoff, temperature, precipitation, potential evapotranspiration, and the normalized difference vegetation index—were compiled for six sub-basins of the Yellow River Basin during 1985–2017. Each variable was decomposed into intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) and a residual component, allowing scale-specific sediment–environment linkages to be identified. The results showed that sediment yield exhibited significant associations at specific scales, including cases where no significant relationship was observed at the observational scale. These controlling relationships were strongly scale-dependent and spatially heterogeneous, with several predictors exerting greater influence at longer time scales. Scale-specific drivers reproduced sediment yield effectively for individual IMFs and residuals, while sediment yield at the observational scale was accurately reconstructed by summing all scale-based predictions. Runoff and precipitation emerged as the dominant predictors in most sub-basins, whereas basin-specific differences were observed for temperature and potential evapotranspiration. MEMD-based modeling substantially improved sediment prediction accuracy (R2 = 0.71–0.93) compared with models using undecomposed data (R2 = 0.37–0.86). These results demonstrate that sediment–environment interactions cannot be fully captured at a single time scale and highlight the potential of MEMD for disentangling multiscale sediment dynamics and improving sediment-yield predictions in large river basins.

title: An analysis of direct and indirect methods of estimating evaporation from a water supply reservoir
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Holly A. Roth, Peter D. Blanken
abstract: Evaporation is an important but often misrepresented or neglected term in managing water supply reservoirs. Many methods are available to estimate evaporation, but it is important to understand the practicality, error, and uncertainty among methods. To address this, we compared evaporation rates from six methods: the eddy covariance technique, a Class-A evaporation pan, an evapotranspiration gauge, the mass-transfer and bulk aerodynamic formulae, and a Bowen ratio estimate for May–October 2020–2024. Since meteorological measurements used for empirical estimates are often land-based, we assessed the influence of fetch on these estimates. Compared to water-fetch conditions, land-fetch winds were weaker (−1.0m s−1) and advected hotter (+0.7°C) and drier (+0.3 kPa, vapor pressure gradient) conditions to the sensors. Taking fetch effects into account, the mass-transfer estimate agreed best with eddy covariance and Bowen ratio estimates on seasonal timescales. A monthly, site-specific coefficient improved total study period evaporation pan-based water balance calculations by an average of 0.5x106 m3 and reduced uncertainty by up to 4% in the summer months. An important finding was the influence of heat storage change and fluctuating water levels on evaporation estimates, as displayed by Bowen ratio estimates. These estimates increased in the fall when water levels were low and stored heat was being released, yet eddy covariance and other methods often decreased. This study exemplified the variability intrinsic to evaporation estimates, but elucidated physical drivers of that variability so managers can make informed decisions that are accessible to their needs.

title: Soil moisture thresholds for runoff generation: depth sensitivity and mechanistic controls
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Zhen Cui, Fuqiang Tian
abstract: A compound wetness index combining antecedent soil moisture and event rainfall (S0 = ASI0 + P) is commonly used to analyze threshold-based runoff responses. However, it remains unclear how the depth of soil moisture integration affects threshold detection and predictive performance. Here, we examined the relationship between runoff thresholds and maximum integration depth (MID) across four experimental catchments spanning diverse climates and runoff generation mechanisms. Using segmented regression across multiple MIDs and monitoring sites, we identified runoff thresholds and evaluated the explanatory power of S0 for stormflow using post-threshold coefficients of determination (Rh 2). Thresholds were consistently detected across integration depths, but explanatory power varies strongly among catchments. In storage-controlled systems, Rh 2 increased with depth, indicating that deeper soil moisture integration better captured subsurface storage controls on stormflow initiation. In contrast, in connectivity-limited or shallow flow-dominated systems, shallow integration depths performed better because near-surface wetting controlled preferential flow or infiltration-excess runoff, whereas deeper integration included hydrologically inactive storage. These results show that the optimal integration depth is catchment dependent and closely linked to dominant runoff generation processes. Accounting for this depth dependence can improve threshold-based runoff analysis and support more process-consistent soil moisture monitoring and hydrological modeling.

title: Consistency of rain storm properties observed by TRMM and GPM for climatological trend analysis
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Xiaoye Fan, Banghai Wu, Yu Wang, Jing Xi, Shi Liu, Yixiao Fu, Zuqian Su
abstract: Precipitation plays an essential role in the Earth’s water and energy cycles. Investigating long-term climatological changes in rainstorm characteristics, such as three-dimensional (3-D) structure, can provide valuable insights into global precipitation variation and the response of multiple complex physical mechanisms within precipitation systems to climate change. In this study, various rainstorm properties observed by the Precipitation Radar onboard the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) satellite and the Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar on the Global Precipitation Measurement Mission (GPM) satellite are compared. The results suggest that the discrepancy in detection ability of weak precipitation between them is expected as the primary cause for the differences in most rainstorm properties. To ensure consistency in the construction of the climatic rainstorm dataset consisting of observations from the two radars, three strategies are employed, including excluding pixels within rainstorms with surface rain rates less than 0.5 mm/h, using specific reflectivity thresholds to indicate the 3-D scales, and choosing characteristic parameters that are less affected by weak precipitation. In addition, the consistency can be further enhanced by selecting those rainstorms with an averaged rain rate exceeding 1.5 mm/h, contributing over 90% of the total global rainfall amount. Finally, a 21-year (2002–2022) rainstorm dataset including 12 highly consistent feature parameters to describe 3-D scale and intensity is constructed for climate trend analysis. Results indicate an increasing horizontal size over tropical land but a decreasing precipitation intensity over the tropical ocean, whereas no significant trend in vertical extent. Additionally, a notable trend disparity exists between the overall rainstorm and its heavy precipitation component, with the latter exhibiting a decreasing horizontal size and an increasing vertical extent in most tropical regions. These findings provide valuable support for the development of a long-term, continuous, and consistent rainstorm feature dataset from satellite observations for precipitation climatology research, contributing to better climate model evaluations and predictions.

title: Integrating petrophysical uncertainty in salinity estimation from ERT and well data using indicator kriging
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Diep Cong-Thi, Ellen Van De Vijver, Linh Pham Dieu, Hieu Ho Huu, Frédéric Nguyen, Thomas Hermans
abstract: Understanding and mapping saltwater intrusion (SI) in coastal aquifers is crucial for safeguarding freshwater resources, yet its spatial characterization remains highly uncertain. Conventional well sampling delivers accurate salinity measurements but is spatially limited, whereas geophysical imaging captures broader subsurface patterns but provides only indirect information constrained by uncertain petrophysical models. To address this, we integrate hydrochemical and geophysical datasets within a probabilistic geostatistical framework. Specifically, total dissolved solids (TDS) concentrations from 70 shallow wells (5–10 m) are combined with electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) data collected along 28 transects in the Luy River catchment, Vietnam. Laboratory experiments established two distinct resistivity–salinity relationships for clay-free and clay-bearing sediments. Uncertainty arises from the unknown clay content at specific locations, representing a key source of ambiguity in petrophysical relationships. Accordingly, each resistivity value was expressed as a probability of exceeding predefined salinity thresholds derived from the TDS distribution. Both a traditional binary indicator transformation and an extended encoding with continuous probabilities were tested. As highlighted by a cross-validation analysis, the combined dataset produces a more consistent and spatially detailed delineation of SI than TDS-only kriging. Moreover, the probabilistic framework explicitly accounts for alternative petrophysical scenarios and quantifies the likelihood of crossing critical salinity limits. This study illustrates the effectiveness of integrating hydrochemical observations with geophysical measurements using indicator kriging to improve the reliability of SI mapping in heterogeneous coastal aquifers.

title: Impact of fire-induced hydrophobic layer formation on hydraulic conductivity in sandy soil
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Shuda Wang, Qihao Li, Vinayak Srivastava, Chen Chen, Hong Je Cho, Haejun Park, Ruiqing Shen, Jaime C. Schussler
abstract: Wildfires alter soil properties and hydrological processes by depleting moisture and forming hydrophobic layers that reduce infiltration and increase runoff. This study used a cone heater to simulate one-dimensional surface heating on sandy soils with and without organic matter and characterized hydrophysical responses through hydraulic conductivity and water vapor adsorption tests. Target temperatures ranging from 100 to 400°C were applied to the samples and achieved when the thermocouple nearest the surface (i.e., 1.27 cm depth) reached the temperature. The hydrophobic layer migrated deeper into the sample as surface heating increased in temperature, and its presence was confirmed through the water vapor adsorption tests. The hydrophobic layer was located between the surface and 1.27 cm depth at 100°C, whereas at 400°C it shifted to the interval between 1.27 and 2.54 cm. Quantitatively, the hydraulic conductivity was reduced by approximately 98% at 100°C and 65% at 400°C. These results offer a reproducible framework for elucidating hydrophobic layer formation, migration, and infiltration response when joined with hydraulic conductivity and water vapor adsorption tests. The results of this study will support improved parameterization of post-wildfire hydrological models and can inform water-resource management in fire-impacted landscapes.

title: A probabilistic modeling framework for data-driven forecasting of rainfall-induced debris flows
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Siling Zhang, Xiaojun Guo, Yong Li, Jianyi Cheng
abstract: Debris flow is often forecast based on relationships between rainfall parameters and debris flow occurrences. The traditional forecasting methods often face the challenges of overreliance on monitored data, high false alarms, and missed detections. This work proposes a probabilistic modeling framework to address such limitations. (1) The Copula method is applied to expand the limited original dataset. (2) A Mixture Model is used to group the data corresponding to the triggering mechanisms, enhancing the physical interpretability; and (3) Triggering thresholds are integrated with Bayesian inference to improve the model’s stability and predictive accuracy. The framework was constructed based on monitoring data of rainfall and debris flow in a small catchment between 2006 and 2023. Compared to conventional binary forecasting models, the proposed model demonstrates superior forecasting precision, particularly under conditions of low-precision input data. It also represents a shift from binary classification to probabilistic forecasting,enabling estimation of the occurrence probability for any given rainfall event. This improvement enhances flexibility and applicability in practical early warning of debris flows.

title: Parameterized physics-informed neural networks for flow reconstruction around idealized islands under data-sparse conditions
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Xiaolong Song, Boliang Liu, Zhong Xiao, Haijue Xu, Yuchuan Bai
abstract: Sustainable management of coastal island environments is often hampered by limited observational data and the high computational cost of resolving complex flow dynamics. This research introduces a parameterized physics–informed neural network (PINN) framework that integrates experimental measurements with flow physics to reconstruct three-dimensional flow fields around islands. The methodology employs a multi-stage training approach: initial learning from domain-wide large eddy simulations, followed by refinement using tomographic particle image velocimetry data, and final optimization across multiple flow regimes. Validation against independent experimental datasets demonstrates robust performance across Reynolds numbers 24,000–96,000, achieving correlation coefficients exceeding 0.9 for primary flow components. Crucially, the framework successfully infers flow characteristics in unmeasured regions, particularly near‑bed zones essential for assessing erosion processes and benthic habitat stability. Analysis reveals complex, regime-dependent relationships between hydrological parameters and wake dynamics that traditional discrete sampling cannot resolve. Specifically, the model identifies an optimal eco-hydrological stability window at intermediate Reynolds numbers ( R e ≈ 48 , 000 ), driven by a stable wake reattachment mechanism that shelters downstream habitats. Furthermore, it quantifies a distinct thrust generation window and significant low-Re flow asymmetry, providing critical insights for sediment transport pathways. The trained model enables rapid generation of: (i) eco-hydrological suitability maps for marine spatial planning, (ii) erosion risk assessments based on bed shear stress distributions, and (iii) hydraulic resistance characterizations for regional scale modeling. This approach offers significant advantages for coastal hydrology by providing high-fidelity field reconstruction from experimental data, offering a valuable tool for water resource management and environmental protection in complex island systems.

title: Persistent performance of the power-function complementary relationship in Earth system models under a warming scenario
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Seokwoo Im, Minha Choi, Daeha Kim
abstract: This study presents a systematic evaluation of the power-function complementary relationship (CR) for estimating global terrestrial evapotranspiration (E) under a high-emission warming scenario. Three parameterization strategies for the exponent b—the polynomial method (b = 2), the combined CR-Budyko framework, and the isenthalpic index approach—were applied independently to atmospheric forcing from eighteen Earth System Models (ESMs) participating in the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) under the SSP5-8.5 pathway over 1980–2100. CR-based E was evaluated against ESM-simulated E at both the global and basin scales to assess the robustness of each parameterization approach across space and time. All three approaches demonstrated strong agreement with the reference E, maintaining basin-scale Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency > 0.88 and Pearson r > 0.95 throughout the study period, even under intensified warming. The polynomial method provided stable and globally neutral performance, with the smallest basin-scale bias across all periods. The CR-Budyko framework most closely reproduced tropical E during the historical period but exhibited growing overestimation under future warming. The isenthalpic index approach most faithfully tracked the global E anomaly trend and performed comparably to the polynomial method in warm and arid regions. The results suggest that the power-function CR provides a physically grounded, calibration-free framework for E assessment in CMIP6 ESMs under warming, while demonstrating that the choice of b parameterization strategy has meaningful implications for regional E estimation across diverse hydroclimatic regimes.

title: Mechanism of differential regulation of hydrogeological parameters ( V and K ) on denitrification (DEN) and dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) under groundwater-surface water interaction
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Xihua Wang, Zejun Liu, Y.Jun Xu, Chaomeng Dai, Rongbing Fu, Nianqing Zhou, Boyang Mao, Shunqing Jia, Chengming Luo
abstract: Due to the differences in hydrological and environmental characteristics, the interaction between groundwater (GW) and surface water (SW) causes the complexity of material migration and transformation in the interaction zone. However, the specific mechanisms by which flow velocity (V) and hydraulic conductivity (K) differentially regulate denitrification (DEN) and dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) through hydraulic retention time remain unclear. This study conducted a series of one-dimensional soil column experiments, through changing the GW-SW interaction mode, V and K, the influence of hydraulic conditions on nitrogen-nitrate migration and transformation was evaluated. Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) methods were applied to study influencing factors of nitrogen migration and transformation. Results showed that during the process of GW recharge SW, higher V and lower K led to an accelerated increase of the growth rate of c(NO3 –-N) in the sediment layer and base soil layer, the equilibrium concentration of c(NO3 –-N) in the sediment layer also increased. c(TN) showed the similar trend and decreased in the reaction equilibrium stage. c(NO2 –-N) and c(NH4 +-N) showed the reverse trend as V decreased and K increased. During the process of SW recharge GW, the decreasing rate of nitrogen concentration accelerated as V increased and K decreased. SHAP analysis identified EC, DOC, pH, Eh and T as the most influential environmental factors governing nitrogen speciation. c(NO3 –-N), c(NO2 –-N) and c(NH4 +-N) was the main factor affecting c(TN). Our key innovation is the systematic decoupling of how V and K differentially regulate DEN and DNRA through hydraulic retention time. Results provided important references for hydrological cycling, nitrogen pollution and control and ecological environmental effects of GW-SW interaction.

title: Thaw slump susceptibility assessment in the central Qinghai–Tibet Plateau permafrost region based on an interpretable 2D-CNN framework with SBAS-InSAR deformation
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Yuting Yang, Rui Wang, Chen Liu, Xia Hu, Jifu Liu, Lianyou Liu, Xiaoyan Li, Hao Zheng
abstract: Permafrost degradation has substantially accelerated the development of thaw slumps in response to climate warming on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP). Thaw slumps represent thermokarst-related hydro-geomorphic features that significantly affect landscape stability and hydrological processes. Thaw slump susceptibility assessment is an effective tool for understanding permafrost landscape responses to climate warming and supporting risk-informed management. However, existing assessments often overlook permafrost surface deformation and the spatially coupled interactions of environmental factors, limiting understanding of thaw slump development mechanisms. In this study, an interpretable two-dimensional convolutional neural network (2D-CNN) framework was employed to assess thaw slump susceptibility, incorporating surface deformation derived from small baseline subset (SBAS) InSAR to capture spatially coupled environmental controls. In addition, the influences of environmental factors were quantitatively analyzed using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) and structural equation modeling (SEM). Results indicate that integrating SBAS-InSAR–derived surface deformation substantially improved thaw slump susceptibility prediction, with the model achieving an AUC of 0.981 and outperforming models without deformation or pixel-based approaches. Based on the susceptibility assessment, incorporating surface deformation enhanced the spatial targeting of high-risk areas, with 177.28 km2 covering 85.23% of mapped thaw slumps, compared with 223.61 km2 and 84.86% without deformation data, indicating a substantial reduction in false-positive predictions. The NDVI, slope, and surface deformation rate were identified as the primary factors associated with thaw slump development, and further analysis revealed that non-linear interactions among these factors are closely related to surface instability. This study presents a robust and interpretable framework for evaluating thaw slump susceptibility, providing new insights into environmental controls while supporting landscape management in permafrost regions.

title: Temporal evolution of stormwater basin soil properties and infiltration rates
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Eimienwanlan Ibhagui, Sara Bonetti, Anthony J. Parolari
abstract: Infiltration-based green stormwater infrastructure (GSI) practices are widely used to mitigate the hydrologic impacts of urbanization. However, how GSI performance evolves over time remains poorly understood. In particular, there is little consensus among published studies on whether GSI infiltration rates increase, decrease, or remain constant as GSI practices age. To address this gap, we hypothesized that GSI soil properties change with age and these changes drive corresponding changes in the infiltration rate. Soil properties and infiltration rates were measured in 28 stormwater infiltration basins along a chronosequence ranging in age from 2 to 20 years. Clay, silt, and organic matter contents increased with age while bulk density decreased with age, suggesting that vegetation and soil biota activity as well as fine sediment accumulation contributed to soil profile evolution. Age, clay, silt, and organic matter correlated with infiltration rate, whereas bulk density and porosity did not. Percent silt content was the best predictor of infiltration rate (R2 = 0.46–0.65, p < 0.001); however, age alone provided moderate predictive power (R2 = 0.16–0.45, p = 0.035–0.001). The best performing single and multiple regression models of infiltration rate used age, organic matter, and silt as predictors (R2 = 0.61–0.65, p < 0.001). These data and models revealed that infiltration rate decreased with basin age and silt content, and increased with organic matter, providing a quantitative link between soil properties and infiltration rate evolution with basin age.

title: Physical mechanisms controlling summer hypoxia hotspots in a large multi-outlet estuary
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Zhenkun Lin, Xiangyu Li, Zheng Chen, Aijun Wang, Jiatang Hu, Jiaxue Wu
abstract: Coastal stratification is traditionally considered the primary physical driver of hypoxia by suppressing vertical mixing and dissolved oxygen (DO) ventilation. However, this classical paradigm often fails in highly dynamic estuaries. Using a validated hydrodynamic-biogeochemical model, we reconstructed summer hypoxia in the Pearl River Estuary (PRE) to investigate the physical mechanisms controlling hotspots in the western (WHZ) and eastern (EHZ) shelf regions. A DO budget analysis reveals that, despite significantly stronger stratification, WHZ exhibits a vertical diffusive DO flux that is twice that of EHZ, making it the overwhelmingly dominant term in bottom physical DO supply. This paradox is driven by tidal straining: in WHZ, intense negative tidal straining (<−1.5 × 10−4 psu2 s−1) disrupts stratification and enhances DO diffusion during the late flood phase, even under low shear stress (<0.1 Pa). In contrast, weak tidal straining in the EHZ leaves DO diffusion governed almost entirely by bottom shear stress. Furthermore, in the EHZ, mixing requires nearly a full tidal cycle; by contrast, tidal straining-induced bottom mixing in the WHZ efficiently penetrates the entire water column within half a tidal cycle, making bottom DO dynamics in WHZ strongly tied to stratification fluctuations. This study provides a physical mechanism that explains the bias in the traditional stratification-controlled DO pattern, thereby improving our ability to manage hypoxia in highly dynamic coastal systems.

title: Disentangling the influence of precipitation on nitrogen loss in the Pearl River Basin
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Xitian Cai, Xiaolu Wu, Haijun Huang, Xuezhi Tan, Zhen Li, Latifah Munirah Kamarudin, Nasir Abbas, Syed Asim Hussain, Li Dan
abstract: Nitrogen loss from terrestrial ecosystems is vital to water quality regulation and ecosystem stability. Understanding its response to precipitation variability is crucial for effective watershed management under climate change. Using nitrogen loss in the Pearl River Basin as a case study, this work advances a novel approach to water quality assessment by applying a state-of-the-art land surface model, Noah-MP-CN, to simulate nitrogen loss under varying precipitation regimes. Results show a strong linear relationship between annual precipitation and nitrogen loss (R2 > 0.7), indicating that long-term hydrological conditions dominate baseline nitrogen export. Extreme rainfall events induce sharp nitrogen fluxes that closely coincide with rainfall peaks and typically account for less than 20% of annual nitrogen loss, serving as important short-term amplifiers. Moreover, precipitation intensity exhibits a nonlinear and time-dependent effect: short-term (7-days) changes have limited impact due to watershed buffering, while sustained increases over longer periods (21 days) significantly enhance nitrogen loss by promoting runoff and nitrogen mobilization. Spatially, higher risks are observed in agricultural areas of the mid- to lower basin. These findings underscore the need to consider both the magnitude and temporal characteristics of precipitation—including intensity and duration—when assessing nitrogen export risks, and to integrate these dynamics into adaptive watershed-scale strategies for water quality protection under future climate extremes.

title: Soil moisture retrieval using multi-system GNSS-IR with a marginal improvement threshold for satellite combination optimization
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Shihai Nie, Xiaoyun Wan, Peng Li, Jinsheng Tu, Xing Wu, Kai Yan
abstract: Global navigation satellite system interferometric reflectometry (GNSS-IR) is widely used for surface soil moisture content (SMC) retrieval. However, under multi-system cooperative observation conditions, an interpretable quantitative criterion for determining the optimal size of multi-satellite combinations remains lacking, limiting the quantitative characterization of information gain and the constraint of combination size. To address this issue, this study proposes a multi-system GNSS-IR soil moisture retrieval method based on a marginal improvement threshold. Within a multi-system collaborative GNSS-IR observation framework, a quantitative relationship between interferometric phase and soil moisture is established. The average pairwise correlation coefficient among satellites is introduced to characterize inter-satellite correlation and information redundancy and to constrain the marginal gain associated with combination size. On this basis, a marginal improvement threshold model is developed to describe the diminishing-return and saturation behavior of retrieval performance with increasing satellite number, thereby providing a tractable criterion for determining the optimal size of multi-system multi-satellite combinations. The results show that multi-system multi-satellite combinations significantly improve GNSS-IR soil moisture retrieval accuracy, while the associated performance gain exhibits diminishing returns and gradually approaches saturation with increasing satellite number. The optimal satellite combination sizes are 5, 7, 10, and 14 for the single-, dual-, triple-, and quadruple-system dual-frequency schemes, respectively. Under the optimal configuration, the quadruple-system dual-frequency multi-satellite scheme achieves R2 values of 0.977 at station P031 and 0.990 at station P387, outperforming all other schemes. These findings provide a quantitative basis for designing multi-system GNSS-IR multi-satellite configurations and a methodological reference for surface hydrological monitoring under complex environmental conditions.

title: Asymmetric evolution of capturability of atmospheric water (CAW) across global arid and humid regions
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Hou-Liang Lu, Hong-Ru Wang, Hui-Min Zuo, Han Zhou, Yu-Fei Jiao, Bill X. Hu
abstract: Global warming has intensified water cycle processes, necessitating the study of atmospheric and terrestrial water dynamics across various arid-humid subregions under climate change. This work introduces the Capturability of Atmospheric Water (CAW) index, which measures the conversion of atmospheric to terrestrial water based on horizontal water vapor transport. We develop a conceptual framework to explore CAW evolution influenced by local and large-scale circulation factors. Our findings reveal significant spatial heterogeneity in CAW across different subregions. Specifically, CAW in semi-arid subregions (with precipitation of 200–600 mm yr−1) shows a marked increase during the cold season (November to March). Conversely, humid regions show a significant decrease in CAW, challenging the “dry gets drier, wet gets wetter” paradigm. Key hydrological variables in semi-arid regions, including precipitation, evaporation, and runoff, have increased, indicating an accelerated hydrological cycle over the past four decades. Our analysis reveals that local CAW changes are influenced by factors such as actual evapotranspiration, surface temperature, wind speed, and cloud cover. Notably, in about 80% (cold season) and 95% (warm season) of grids, there is a negative correlation between potential evapotranspiration and CAW, suggesting that increased atmospheric evapotranspiration capacity hinders the conversion of atmospheric water to precipitation. At a larger scale, CAW changes are influenced by large-scale circulation patterns, with equatorial Pacific Sea surface temperature anomalies playing a significant role in most of the semi-arid regions at low and middle latitudes. These findings have important implications for regional water resource management and climate adaptation strategies.

title: Representing glacier evolution for modelling hydrological responses to climate change in mountainous catchments
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Denis Ruelland, Florian Antoine, Antoine Rabatel
abstract: This paper presents the integration of a glacier evolution scheme into the spatially distributed Snow and Ice Accounting Routine (SIAR) and its coupling with a daily runoff model to assess the influence of glacier recession on streamflow in glacierized catchments of the French Alps. Glacier changes are simulated using the Δh parameterization within SIAR, allowing dynamic representation of glacier area and ice mass evolution. Model calibration follows a multi-criteria strategy combining streamflow, snow water equivalent (SWE), remotely sensed snow and ice cover, and glacier areas for 1967–2024. SWE and glacier extent data are shown to be key for constraining accumulation, melt, and long-term mass balance. Despite incorporating glacier evolution, only a few hydrological parameters require calibration, demonstrating the feasibility of a parsimonious yet process-based representation of snow and ice. In particular, adjusting precipitation inputs for orographic effects and wind under-catch reduces parameter complexity while maintaining consistency across multiple variables. Although accounting for glacier evolution does not systematically improve streamflow metrics, it enhances the physical realism of simulated snow and ice processes. Results also reveal two distinct hydrological responses depending on glacier coverage: in highly glacierized catchments (>15%), sustained meltwater input continues to support summer flows, indicating that peak water has not yet been reached; in contrast, catchments with limited glacier extent exhibit a shift toward snow-dominated regimes and reduced summer runoff. These contrasting behaviours highlight differences in glacier storage capacity and response time, emphasizing the importance of accounting for evolving cryospheric processes in hydrological modelling under climate change.

title: Effective risks and dominant factors of drought-flood abrupt alternation events to global socio-ecological systems
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Bohua Wu, Ziqi Yan, Denghua Yan, Yaping Cheng, Baisha Weng, Jianzhu Li
abstract: Drought-flood abrupt alternation (DFAA) events are an important manifestation of instability in the global climate system and pose substantial risks to society and ecosystems. However, the risks that DFAA events impose on affected systems have not yet been systematically quantified at the global scale. Based on the three key components of hazard, exposure, and vulnerability, this study applies a multiplicative model to assess global DFAA risk, develops a “double-mean, double-threshold, and double-driver” analytical framework, quantifies the effective risks of DFAA events to social and ecological systems, and identifies their major influencing factors. The results showed that, although the global mean DFAA hazard increased slightly, regional differences are pronounced. The social system exhibited a pattern of increasing exposure and decreasing vulnerability, whereas the ecosystem showed simultaneous increases in both exposure and vulnerability. Although the spatial extent of flood-to-drought risk was smaller than that of drought-to-flood risk, it was more destructive in some regions. The overall centroid of social system risk shifted toward the southeast and southwest, whereas that of ecosystem risk shifted toward the northeast. The mechanisms driving risk also showed pronounced asymmetry, with socio-ecological system factors dominating during the drought-to-flood stage and climatic factors playing a leading role during the flood-to-drought stage. Overall, this study reveals the differences in DFAA risk and the asymmetric driving characteristics affecting social and ecological systems at the global scale, providing a scientific basis for risk warning, adaptive management, and sustainable development decision-making related to DFAA events.

title: Revealing irregular sediment shape effects in bedload transport rate based on state probability correction
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Yipin Nie, Xiekang Wang
abstract: Sediment transport processes not only reshape river channel geomorphology but also directly influence the accuracy of flood routing and watershed ecological management. However, bedload transport calculations in traditional hydrological models are predominantly based on the assumption of ideal spherical particles, often neglecting the irregular shapes of sediment in natural channels. This simplification limits the models’ ability to interpret and predict sediment motion mechanisms under complex hydrodynamic conditions. Building upon existing theories of sediment motion state probability, this study modifies the classical computational framework by introducing the Corey shape factor (Sf). This modification employs Markov chain processes to quantify the transition probabilities of sediment particles between different motion states. It focuses on correcting physical parameters—specifically the effective frontal projected area, settling velocity, and drag coefficient—for irregular particles, thereby integrating microscopic shape effects into macroscopic transport rate calculations. Validation against approximately 1,650 experimental datasets covering a wide range of transport intensities (dimensionless sediment transport intensity Φ ranging from 10-4 to 103) demonstrates that the corrected method captures how sediment irregularity significantly enhances the capacity of particles to extract energy from the flow by increasing the drag coefficient and frontal projected area. Under specific flow intensities, the transport rates of irregular particles can be tens of times higher under specific flow intensities. Furthermore, applying this modified framework to the numerical simulation of a flood event in the Xiaoshi River reveals that, compared to traditional formulas, the corrected model more physically plausibly represents the riverbed surface armoring process and the dynamic adjustment of the longitudinal grain size distribution during the flood. This study confirms that explicitly correcting for sediment shape effects in numerical models holds critical hydrological significance for improving the reliability of riverbed evolution predictions under unsteady flow conditions, providing a more physically grounded computational basis for quantifying watershed sediment flux and for engineering design.

title: Application of real-time data assimilation system to improve streamflow forecasts in Japan
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Yingying Liu, Kei Yoshimura, Menaka Revel, Yuting Zhu
abstract: Accurate and timely flood forecasting is vital for effective water management and disaster mitigation. Data assimilation (DA) can improve hydrodynamic model performance by integrating real-time observations, yet its practical use at national scale remains limited. This study presents the first development of a real-time online DA system in Japan for a large-scale hydrodynamic model, assimilating hourly water surface elevation (WSE) observations from 1800 in-situ gauges across the country. The system employs the Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter (LETKF), which updates model states using only spatially relevant observations. This localization expands DA coverage from 10% to 58.4% by leveraging nearby gauges to correct conditions even at non-observed locations. System performance was evaluated across three major flood events in Japan and assessed on WSE, river discharge, and inundation extent. At assimilated stations, DA improved WSE accuracy at 78%-95% of stations. For discharge, 65% of stations improved, with over 60% achieving a Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) above 0.5, demonstrating benefits for non-assimilated variables as well. When assimilating only surrounding gauges, over 80% of stations still showed improved WSE. Forecasting skill was also enhanced. In events with relatively good open-loop (OL) predictions, DA outperformed OL simulations for lead times of up to 5 hours. In events with poor OL predictions, DA consistently enhanced forecasts one-day-ahead. Comparison with SAR-derived flood extent further confirmed improved inundation mapping within 24-hour lead times, as DA results exhibited reduced overestimation relative to OL. These results demonstrate a practical real-time DA framework for national-scale flood forecasting and management.

title: Explainable physics-informed Bayesian graph neural networks (PI-BSTGNN) for groundwater surrogate modeling and sensitivity analysis
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Fan Liu, Zhao Guo, Futian Ren, Hassina Mouri, Danbing Mei, Zhengzheng Zhang, Xiaowei Lu, Lei Huang
abstract: Groundwater contamination from industrial and agricultural sources threatens sustainable development. To bridge the gap between expensive mechanistic models and physics-agnostic data-driven methods, we propose PI-BSTGNN, a Physics-Informed Bayesian Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network. Using MODFLOW6 to generate 100 stochastic realizations of a 3D heterogeneous aquifer system, we embed hydrodynamic constraints (mass conservation, Dirichlet boundaries) directly into the loss function. Evaluated on a 3D random-field heterogeneity case, the framework achieves a head RMSE of 3.61 m (R2 = 0.896) and a concentration RMSE of 1.02 mg/L (R2 = 0.864). Out-of-Distribution (OOD) tests reveal that the physics-informed anchor maintains a head R2 of 0.663, while standard CNN and RF models diverge catastrophically (R2 < 0). Furthermore, two-stage training proved essential for concentration accuracy, preventing error propagation from velocity fields. SHAP analysis reveals that aquifer geometry and river boundaries are dominant drivers. These results demonstrate that PI-BSTGNN provides a scalable, physically consistent, and uncertainty-aware surrogate for sustainable groundwater management.

title: Groundwater level recovery drives soil nitrate losses into groundwater: evidence from integrated modeling and statistical analysis
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Yongge Zang, Hong Yu, Xu Han, Xinjuan Wang, Yu Yang, Yonghai Jiang
abstract: Abundant soil nitrate (NO3 −) have been reported to be accumulated in regions where both the thick vadose zone (TVZ) and intensive agricultural cultivation prevail. The residual NO3 − profoundly disrupts terrestrial nitrogen cycles and poses a serious threat to groundwater quality. In particular, the groundwater level (GWL) in these regions, driven by mitigation countermeasures for groundwater depletion, were greatly elevated over recent years, thereby further exacerbating the pollution risk mentioned above. Nevertheless, it remains indistinct how soil NO3 − stock in the TVZ respond to this large-scale GWL recovery and whether the underlying regulatory mechanism for their losses is affected at a regional scale. Aimed at this problem, this study established a process-oriented integrated model for the vadose zone-groundwater coupled system in a typical GWL recovery region, followed by multi-variable statistical analysis including correlation analysis, random forest and structural equation modeling. The attained results classified soil NO3 − losses across the entire vadose zone into two distinct pathways: leaching driven by water infiltration, and mobilization via physical displacement and hydrodynamic mixing into rising groundwater. The amount of these two losses, triggered by the GWL recovery, increased by 0.74 times and 2.35 times, respectively. Moreover, the mobilization losses gradually replaced the leaching ones as the dominant component of soil NO3 − losses. In addition, the GWL recovery has superseded the original critical driver, soil NO3 − stock, to become the new primary driver of soil NO3 − losses. More importantly, the encounter between soil NO3 − content peak and groundwater, stimulated by the GWL recovery, also occurred 0.36–0.79 times earlier, particularly in areas characterized by substantial GWL rise, coarse soil textures, and a thin vadose zone. Appropriate recharge schemes and soil NO3 − reduction strategies are therefore urgently required to alleviate the adverse effects associated with the GWL recovery.

title: A two-stage data fusion framework for multi-source precipitation estimates integrating gauge, radar, and satellite observations via deep learning and Bayesian model averaging
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Lijun Chao, Tingting Hou, Sheng Wang, Zhixin He, Ke Zhang, Guoqing Wang
abstract: Reliable precipitation estimation over complex terrain requires the integration of complementary information from rain gauges, weather radar, and satellite products. Effective data fusion remains challenging due to scale inconsistencies, spatial heterogeneity, and source-dependent uncertainties. We propose a transparent two-stage deep-learning–Bayesian multi-source precipitation fusion framework (DBMPF) integrating spatiotemporal deep-learning (DL) correction with probabilistic ensemble calibration. The first stage employs a hybrid 3-dimensional convolutional neural network (3D-CNN) and convolutional long short-term memory (ConvLSTM) architecture to extract station-centered spatiotemporal features from multi-source data cubes and to produce corrected member ensemble members corresponding to different source combinations. The second stage applies Bayesian model averaging (BMA) to merge these members into a calibrated predictive distribution through the expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm. A Box-Cox transformation is introduced to better satisfy Gaussian residual assumptions, facilitating uncertainty quantification through prediction intervals and probabilistic evaluation metrics. The DBMPF framework is assessed in the Tunxi River basin (Anhui, China) during May–September, trained on 2019–2020, and validated in 2022 for validation at daily, hourly, and half-hourly temporal resolutions. Across all scales, DBMPF surpasses both the source products and benchmark approaches. At the daily scale, the correlation coefficient (CC) increases from 0.942 for radar to 0.994,root mean square error (RMSE) decreases from 5.231 to 1.685 mm/day, and Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) rises from 0.750 to 0.972, accompanied by negligible bias. At sub-daily resolutions, improvements are observed in event detection performance as measured by critical success index (CSI) and false alarm ratio (FAR), and the framework achieves superior probabilistic performance for 95% prediction intervals, attaining the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), PICP values closest to the nominal 0.95 level, and the smallest absolute coverage error (ACE) across precipitation intensity categories while maintaining relatively narrow mean prediction interval width (MPIW). A progressive gauge-density experiment involving 18–45 stations reveals substantial performance gains under sparse observational networks and diminishing returns at moderate to high densities, offering guidance for cost-efficient network configuration. The proposed DBMPF framework provides a modular approach for generating high-resolution deterministic and probabilistic precipitation estimates, with particular potential for flood-focused hydrological applications requiring uncertainty-aware precipitation inputs.

title: A novel hybrid modeling-based artificial intelligence agent for water-food-ecology-environment-economy system trade-offs
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Yue Li, Zhijun Chen, Min Hu, Xinyi Li, Yufei Han, Dongyang Ren, Xu Xu, Yunwu Xiong, Quanzhong Huang, Guanhua Huang
abstract: The mismanagement of irrigation, fertilization, and cropping systems intensifies conflicts within the Water-Food-Ecology-Environment-Economy (WFEEE) system.
