abstract: The inset

title: Groundwater-based water services as complex socio-hydrogeological systems: insights from Vietnam’s Mekong Delta
abstract: Abstract Groundwater systems are critical to global water security, yet the complex interactions between household coping strategies, resource sustainability, and climate change remain difficult to govern. This study applies qualitative systems mapping to characterise socio-hydrogeological dynamics in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta, a region currently facing intensifying saline intrusion and rapid land-use change. Drawing on a household survey ( n = 404) and in-depth interviews ( n = 25) in Sóc Trăng and Trà Vinh provinces, three critical system interactions were identified: (1) climate variability and household adaptation intensify groundwater system pressures, (2) policy-practice gaps undermine effective management of a multisource water system, and (3) social vulnerability and water stress constrain resilience. Together, these interactions illustrate how household behaviours, institutional arrangements, and resource conditions are interconnected in ways that shape system behaviour. These findings advance socio-hydrogeological frameworks by using systems mapping to make visible the relationships and interactions that influence groundwater-based water services. The research offers evidence for policymakers, suggesting that inclusive, climate-resilient service delivery depends on integrating actual household water behaviours into planning and groundwater governance, moving beyond a singular focus on piped supply.

title: Comparative analysis of lineament mapping using Sentinel-1A, Landsat 8 OLI, and ALOS PALSAR for hydrogeological applications in the Moroccan Central Massif
Risk assessment of tunnelling-induced hydrogeological interference on springs using a machine learning approach
abstract: Abstract Tunnel excavation through mountain ranges can alter groundwater regimes, affecting spring discharge and dependent ecosystems. Anticipating these interferences is essential for environmental risk management, cost–benefit analysis, and effective mitigation planning. Conventional assessment methods are largely parametric, not physically based, and heavily dependent on expert judgment, introducing subjectivity and uncertainty. This study proposes a data-driven approach based on machine learning (ML), specifically a Random Forest (RF) model, to evaluate hydrogeological risk and spring vulnerability during the preliminary design phase of tunnels. The method exploits geological information typically available in early stages and is validated using two well-documented Italian case studies: The Bologna–Florence high-speed railway line, excavated in fractured sedimentary formations of the Northern Apennines, and the Gran Sasso highway tunnels, driven in karstified carbonate rocks of the Central Apennines. Both datasets are published, hydrogeologically validated, and supported by detailed pre- and post-excavation monitoring, ensuring robustness and consistency. The ML framework demonstrates strong predictive performance across standard classification metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and area under the curve (AUC). While it employs input parameters comparable to those of parametric methods such as the drawdown hazard index (DHI), it differs by deriving parameter weights directly from data. Moreover, the use of Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values enhances interpretability, mitigates black-box behaviour, and allows expert knowledge to be effectively integrated. The innovation, therefore, lies in offering a transferable and reproducible tool to support early-stage tunnelling decisions, representing a clear improvement over traditional qualitative or semi-quantitative approaches.

title: Quantitative evaluation on non-Darcian flow and non-Fickian transport: Visualization experiments on fracture networks
Effect of flow velocity and contact area on solute transport in rock fractures
Karst hydraulic scale effect in confined and unconfined zones of the Neoproterozoic Sete Lagoas Karst Aquifer System (Brazil)
abstract: Résumé L'effet d'échelle de la perméabilité karstique décrit la variation des paramètres hydrauliques mesurés à différentes échelles spatiales, en réponse à l'hétérogénéité et à la structure de porosité complexe des aquifères karstiques. À Sete Lagoas (État du Minas Gerais, Brésil), le système aquifère karstique néoprotérozoïque de Sete Lagoas (SLKAS) comprend des zones captives et libres. La compréhension de cet effet d'échelle sous différentes conditions hydrostatiques est essentielle pour affiner les modèles conceptuels d'écoulement, l'estimation des paramètres et la gestion des eaux souterraines dans de tels systèmes hétérogènes. Cet article intègre des investigations en laboratoire et sur le terrain, combinant des essais de perméamétrie, des essais à charge variable avec injection instantanée, des essais de pompage de longue durée et des analyses régionales avec délimitation de la zone d’alimentation, afin d'estimer la perméabilité, la conductivité hydraulique et la transmissivité à quatre échelles spatiales : matrice (< 10⁻² m), petite échelle (10⁻²– 10 0 m), puits (10 0 –10³ m) et régionale (> 10³ m). Les résultats montrent une augmentation de la perméabilité de quatre à six ordres de grandeur entre la matrice et la petite échelle, suivie d'une diminution à l'échelle du puits et d'une nouvelle augmentation à l'échelle régionale. Ce modèle non linéaire à plusieurs échelles diffère des systèmes karstiques récents classiques, où la perméabilité augmente généralement de façon progressive avec l'échelle. La partie captive du SLKAS présente des valeurs de perméabilité inférieures d'un à deux ordres de grandeur à celles de la zone libre, reflétant une karstification et une connectivité réduites sous l'influence de facteurs tectono-structuraux et stratigraphiques. Ces résultats offrent une nouvelle approche multi-échelle intégrant les méthodes de laboratoire et de terrain pour quantifier les effets d'échelle hydraulique sous différentes conditions de pression hydrostatique, et les comparent à ceux observés dans des systèmes karstiques plus récents.

title: Community views on hydrogeology education: A global perspective from 2024
abstract: Abstract Groundwater is the Earth’s largest reservoir of available freshwater. As climate change and increasing anthropogenic pressures continue to affect its availability and quality, the discipline of hydrogeology is evolving rapidly. Training enough professionals capable of understanding and managing groundwater resources effectively is therefore more critical than ever. However, there is a perceived global shortage of adequately trained hydrogeologists—raising concerns about society’s capacity to address future groundwater-related challenges. To obtain quantitative data regarding this perception and to evaluate the current state of hydrogeology education and workforce dynamics more generally, a global survey was conducted of hydrogeology professionals, recent graduates, and current students. Five hundred seventy-three individuals from 82 countries responded, providing contemporary insights into the discipline’s demographics, education pathways, and perceived training gaps. Here, a synthesis of the key findings is presented—offering a snapshot of current trends and challenges in hydrogeology education from various perspectives. Notable findings include the observations that: (i) female hydrogeologists remain underrepresented; (ii) some countries act as major “exporters” or “importers” of hydrogeologists; (iii) many practitioners consider new graduates to be insufficiently prepared; (iv) most hydrogeological work is conducted by those without formal education in the field; and (v) hydrogeology is expected to contribute to a growing range of challenges, calling for both disciplinary depth and interdisciplinary breadth in curricula. These findings highlight a need for better alignment between academic training and professional demands. The full dataset is openly shared, offering a resource for educators, researchers, and policymakers to support training and engagement with global water issues.
